AI has taken the world by storm, and the data centers behind broad AI adoption threaten society on multiple fronts. Or so it seems. Read the (un)ugly truth and decide whether AI will be friend or foe.

In October 2024, I wrote, “Artificial Intelligence from Behind the Curtain.” The article offered some insight into how AI works and whether the dangers come from AI or the humans using it. Two years and a few thousand AI data centers down the road, what has changed?

While AI is now on every front page, in politics, web search, shopping, industry, and just about every popular app, the grassroots are mobilizing against the data centers that fuel AI. There are fears that data centers will overload our aging electricity grid and drive up power costs. That they will use up precious fresh water in arid states. That they create harmful infrasound, eliminate jobs, and enable fraud. Most importantly, that AI’s output is inaccurate at best and hallucinatory at worst. Yet, AI data center growth continues with such reckless abandon that the only possible endgame is an AI industry crash that will pull the world economy down with it into a recession like we haven’t seen since 2008, maybe longer.

Related:Best Undergraduate College Programs for Artificial Intelligence

Should we all panic? No. Should we be up in arms? No. Is it a conspiracy? No. Let me explain why.

The biggest problem with data centers is that, relative to most industrial construction, they are a simple design. Take a processor with good parallel processing capability, memory, power supply, and I/O and replicate it a few thousand times. From there you need to manage power in and heat out and signals in, out, and about.

The first modern (non-mainframe-based) data centers were built by networking large numbers of conventional desktop PCs together. Later came gaming GPU-based servers, and now modular AI-targeted mass-manufactured servers. The use of COTS (common off-the-shelf) components enables easy, fast growth but does not lead to an efficient system. Small losses that are perfectly acceptable for an individual home PC or enterprise server combine to create existentially significant inefficiencies when a facility is drawing gigawatts of power.

To date, little more than money and a general contractor are all that is needed to build an AI data center. You don't need leading-edge expertise. Just money—and there is a lot of money in the community of companies that want to build data centers. That group has further increased the available funding with circular financing (I’ll pay now for your future GPUs if you pay now for my future processing cycles).

As I write this, the AI industry is running well ahead of the government and self-regulatory environments. That means that data center construction and bring-up time is the primary driver. Not accuracy. Not code efficiency, not financial efficiency. It’s just a full speed race. AI companies are throwing up data centers willy-nilly without much strategic thought to water or electricity. About $3-7 trillion in data center infrastructure is in the works, and data centers now account for roughly half of all new power grid demand. Cities and states are starting to call “uncle.” Several have already thrown moratoriums on new datacenter licenses or are working to outright ban them.

Related:AI Ushers in a New Age of Creativity for Engineers

Over-regulation and a strong public backlash may seem like a death knell to a burgeoning industry. At face value, maybe so, but the reality is that the high-tech industry tends to jump and run at the first inclination of a good idea. That works in the early days but, as with all innovation, the industry starts with speed but eventually must transition to efficiency.

While efficiency has been a part of electronics design for decades, hyperscale efficiency—a level adequate for modern data center installations—is not yet here. GPUs typically hit about 30% utilization due to memory bandwidth limitations and peak/valley demand. Power supplies give up between three and six percent of their power to waste heat. That leaves a lot of room for improvement. By putting brakes on data centers now, the industry will not give up. It will retool for efficiency, and the resulting changes will lead to better results, faster, with greater accuracy, for a much lower financial and environmental cost.

I am reminded of a passage in the 1974 techno-philosophy tome, Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance. The author, Robert Pirsig, wrote that pioneers are, “by their very nature, mess-makers. They go forging ahead, seeing only their noble, distant goal, and never notice any of the crud and debris they leave behind them.”

Pirsig was referring broadly to pioneers of all sorts throughout time. It is no different in technology today. It would be nice if it were, but it is not. AI is in that pioneering stage, and they are making a mess of it. Public outcry and policy legislation are starting the cleanup phase. In half a decade, most of the cleanup (bringing in environmental and fiscal efficiency) will be completed or well underway.

Likely half or more of the current set of AI “gold rushers" will be out of business by the early 2030s. Those who remain will have learned to do it right. Between more efficient power distribution/management, more efficient silicon, and more efficient algorithms, the data centers will have at least 10x the output per Watt as today’s.

Agentic AI (AAI) will surpass generative AI in terms of processing cycles. But it requires a different set of processing capabilities. Today’s AI is largely about MAC (multiply accumulate) operations, and Nvidia is the clear leader in MAC capability. But MACs will become a commodity. MACs will become the “MLCC (multi-layer ceramic capacitor) popcorn” component of AI data centers as AI fractionalizes into more specialized categories and as AAI builds and subsumes whole classes of activity.

AAI requires intensive unsupervised interpretation of text, imagery, and sensor input; LLM reference; chain of thought (CoT) reasoning; and retrieval augmented generation (RAG). In addition to MAC units, AAI requires heavy conventional processing for task assignment and management. While most LLM-based AI lives on low precision, AAI will equally need high-precision math. There is a lot of room for new silicon entrants.

The good of AI includes significant wins in our near future. Some of these are possible now and some are close. All will be viable solutions within the next five years and common shortly after that:

You walk up to your home’s front door, and it unlocks and opens for you. No key. No code. No setting down grocery bags. Just a simple AI-based recognition. And if you say it’s okay for Cousin Avery to stop by between eight and ten on Tuesday morning, they get the same treatment. So do your pets. No one else does unless you say so. This technology all exists today. It just needs someone to integrate and sell it. It will be productized in the USA and mass-produced in Asia soon.

Your best friend’s cancer is caught months before a human would have been able to spot it on the x-ray. Thanks to the early diagnosis, treatment is quick and successful with limited invasiveness. Studies are already underway confirming this capability. Certification awaits. Expect this in the USA first and Europe second.

Instead of HOV (high occupancy vehicle) lanes, most cities will create self-driving level-4+ (SD4+) capable vehicle lanes. Within these lanes, cars will communicate and travel faster and closer together. The collective set will automatically open and close gaps for additional SD4+ vehicles to join or exit. Overall road capacity will increase, and accidents will decrease without a significant construction burden. Most of the technology is available at least in prototype form.
